"executive_summary": "This study investigates the intracellular signaling of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor, CTGF) in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor, but its roles in lymphangiogenesis remained unclear. Using primary cultured LECs, the authors found that CCN2 upregulated lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but not at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 significantly increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001) without affecting total ERK, and this effect was partially mediated by integrin av, since knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Although CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth, it enhanced the interaction between ERK and dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), which dephosphorylates ERK; knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed that exogenous CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels and induced phospho-ERK-positive and DUSP6-positive LECs. These results suggest that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6, which enables negative modulation of ERK-signaling. The study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding CCN2 signaling in lymphangiogenesis and identifies integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets for lymphatic diseases such as oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).",

summary.title: CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av and enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in lymphatic endothelial cells
summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi, Tomoko Tanaka, Ryosuke Mano, Seiji Kondo, Shohta Kodama (Fukuoka University)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the intracellular signaling of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor, CTGF) in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor, but its roles in lymphangiogenesis remained unclear. Using primary cultured LECs, the authors found that CCN2 upregulated lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but not at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 significantly increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001) without affecting total ERK, and this effect was partially mediated by integrin av, since knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Although CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth, it enhanced the interaction between ERK and dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), which dephosphorylates ERK; knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed that exogenous CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels and induced phospho-ERK-positive and DUSP6-positive LECs. These results suggest that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6, which enables negative modulation of ERK-signaling. The study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding CCN2 signaling in lymphangiogenesis and identifies integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets for lymphatic diseases such as oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the intracellular signaling of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor, CTGF) in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor, but its roles in lymphangiogenesis remained unclear. Using primary cultured LECs, the authors found that CCN2 upregulated lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but not at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 significantly increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001) without affecting total ERK, and this effect was partially mediated by integrin av, since knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Although CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth, it enhanced the interaction between ERK and dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), which dephosphorylates ERK; knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed that exogenous CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels and induced phospho-ERK-positive and DUSP6-positive LECs. These results suggest that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6, which enables negative modulation of ERK-signaling. The study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding CCN2 signaling in lymphangiogenesis and identifies integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets for lymphatic diseases such as oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

Research Context
CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor. CCN2 contains four structural domains including the TSP domain. CCN2 activates MAPKs such as p38 MAPK, ERK, and JNK. CCN2 interacts with integrins via its TSP and C-terminal domains. CCN2 is closely associated with lymphangiogenesis in fibrous diseases. CCN2 signaling in LECs in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether CCN2 regulates lymphangiogenesis in LECs. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs. The authors hypothesized that CCN2-mediated ERK activation involves integrins. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 enhances ERK-DUSP6 interaction. The authors hypothesized that DUSP6 negatively modulates ERK-signaling. The authors predicted that CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo.

Methodological Details
Primary LECs were derived from C57BL/6 mice. LECs were cultured in EGM2 medium at 37°C with 5% CO2. Cells up to 6 passages were used in in vitro experiments. LECs were stimulated with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100 or 200 ng/mL of CCN2. Gene expression was analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. Phospho-RTKs were analyzed using a phospho-RTK array. Integrin mRNAs were examined in primary LECs treated with CCN2. Integrins and DUSP6 were suppressed by siRNA. siRNAs were designed using siDirect ver.2. Protein expression was analyzed by Western blot. Total protein was incubated with receptor-spotted membrane for RTK array. Immunoprecipitation used anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6 antibodies. Male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used for in vivo assays. Mice were euthanized at day 7 after injection. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism version 8. Statistical significance was set at a p-value of less than 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
Cell proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining. Cells were plated at 2 × 10^4 cells per well. Absorbance at 590 nm was measured using the SPARK 10M plate reader. Cell proliferation was expressed as the ratio to the absorbance at 0 h. Total RNA was prepared using the Purelink RNA purification Kit. cDNA was prepared from 1 μg of total RNA. Quantitative RT-PCR used TB Green Premix ExTaq II. LECs were pre-cultured with FBS-free medium for 24 h. Protein samples of 5-20 µg were separated with SDS-PAGE. The membrane was blocked in Blocking-one for 30 min. Primary antibodies were incubated at 4°C overnight. Secondary antibodies were incubated for 2 h. Signals were quantified using ImageQuant TL 8.1 software. Growth factor reduced Matrigel was mixed with recombinant rat CCN2. 450 µL of Matrigel and 8.33 µg of CCN2 were injected. Sections 4 µm thick were deparaffinized and stained with HE. Confocal microscopy used the LSM710 microscope. All experiments were performed more than three times.

Key Results
CCN2 upregulated Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1 in a dose-dependent manner. At 200 ng/mL, marker expression dramatically decreased. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd and Flt4 but not Kdr. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged by CCN2. EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation were increased by CCN2. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2 (p<0.001). Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2. Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs. Knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Knockdown of integrin a9 slightly increased phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1 (p=0.05). Dusp6 was predominant among DUSPs in LECs. DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001 at 15 min). Phospho-ERK was increased at 15 min and up to 4 h. Phospho-ERK-positive LECs were detected in CCN2 plugs. DUSP6-positive LECs were detected in CCN2 plugs. The number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by CCN2. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression were increased in CCN2 gel (p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av in LECs. CCN2 enhances the binding between ERK and DUSP6. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK-signaling. DUSP6 suppresses excessive activation of ERK. Integrin av, ERK and DUSP6 may be therapeutic targets of OSCC. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not been analyzed.

Contradictions And Limitations
CCN2 weakly suppressed LEC proliferation in vitro. CCN2 enhanced lymphangiogenesis in vivo Matrigel assays. The discrepancy may be due to effects of ECM and MMP. The results between these assays may not be comparable. Integrin b1 loss was not compensated by integrins b2 and b3. Integrin a5 is increased by suppression of integrin b1. The interaction between CCN2 and integrin a5 has not been reported. The exact number of mice per group is not specified. The study used only C57BL/6 mice.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av in LECs. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2. Knockdown of integrin av reduced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed. Knockdown of integrin a9 slightly increased phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1. Integrin av is a key mediator of CCN2 signaling. Integrin av may be a therapeutic target.
CCN2 enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6, which negatively modulates ERK-signaling. DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001). DUSP6 is highly expressed in LECs. CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not been analyzed. DUSP6 suppresses excessive activation of ERK. DUSP6 may be a therapeutic target.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo via Matrigel plug assay. The number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression were increased (p<0.05). Tubular structures were observed in CCN2 gels. The discrepancy may be due to effects of ECM and MMP. The results between these assays may not be comparable. CCN2 positively modulated lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 may be relevant to OSCC progression.

Data And Code Availability
Primers are listed in Table S1. siRNA sequences are listed in Table S2. Antibodies are listed in Table S3. Supplementary figures are provided (Fig. S1-S4).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
All experiments were performed more than three times. The RTK assay was performed with n=2. Knockdown of integrin av reduced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001). Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK (p=0.05).

Ethical Considerations
All experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee. Experiments complied with relevant laws and institutional guidelines. Approval number was 2008024.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1A showed dose-dependent upregulation of Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1. Fig. 1B showed increased Vegfc, Vegfd and Flt4. Fig. 2A showed increased phospho-ERK by CCN2. Fig. 3B showed reduced phospho-ERK by integrin av knockdown. Fig. 4A showed weak growth inhibition by CCN2. Fig. 5B showed DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK. Fig. 6A showed blood vessels in CCN2 plugs. Fig. 7A showed phospho-ERK in CCN2 gel.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of CCN2-ERK-DUSP6 signaling in LECs. 2. The strongest evidence is the integrin av knockdown reducing phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). 3. The future path is analyzing FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 relationships.
